chapter: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
title: Django Reinhardt's economy and jazz as statement, painting or poetry
summary: He describes how Django found notes equal to twenty others, and divides jazz players into those who make statements, babble, paint or are poets like Buck Clayton.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: So, and Djang, Djang, well, Djang was there and Tango had, he was, he had a problem as we all have heard about. But he could find what he was missing in his physical incapacity because he had mentally -- he would come to a passage
that he knew it meant a lot of execution, but he would find a note as you would call a oul note, which would equal twenty notes to the other person's one.
You've got to watch that type of man. That is why Jango he always, his statements, see, what I believe when you playing jazz, you make a statement or you paint a picture.
Or, if you are a poet, to a jazz man, either they make statements -- some of them babble, some of them are painters, some of them paint poetry, and are poets, see.

But, now, Buck Clayton is a poet. So, Djangó, and -- they all used to play together. All of them played together and when Oscar made something pretty, Djangó would -- hee, hee, hee, he had that little funny smile and Oscar would say, please -- wait a minute, then, right through that little drink of Pernot. At that time, pernot was a good -- was the drink --
